newsitem.title: USA: Progress seen on U.S. budget but no deal imminent.
newsitem.headline: Progress seen on U.S. budget but no deal imminent.

text.p: White House officials and two top senators suggested Thursday that efforts to reach a balanced budget agreement are making progress but said that a deal was neither certain nor imminent.

Republican Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a key player in the budget endgame, said the White House and congressional Republicans were coming closer to one another, particularly on the issue of tax cuts.

"I think we are working toward each other. They are coming up, we are coming down," Lott said, effectively conceding that the nearly $200 billion in tax cuts that the Republicans had originally wanted were unlikely to materialise.

President Clinton met top Democratic senators at the White House Thursday in an effort to reassure the members of his party that he will not cut them out of any accord that he may reach with the Republicans who control Congress.
Asked afterward about speculation that a deal might be struck early next week, Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle told reporters: "I would say today that's unlikely."
"I wish that were true ... I'm not sure that anyone can say with any certainty that we're going to get it," he added.
Earlier in the day, however, he had told reporters "there appears to be movement" in the talks between the White House and Congress.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry also suggested that it will take more time for any agreement. "We're moving forward with the talks," McCurry told reporters. "They're working very hard and we'll see where they end up in the coming weeks."

The White House and congressional Republicans are locked in negotiations over how to balance the budget by 2002, with the key issues including the size of a tax cut and the extent of cuts to the Medicare health care programme for the elderly.

In one sign of how precarious part of Medicare's financing is, the trustees of its hospital insurance trust fund, which helps pay for inpatient hospital care for many people over 65, said on Thursday the fund could go bankrupt by 2001.
On taxes, Clinton's budget proposed gross tax cuts of $98 billion over five years while Republicans want significantly more and had initially sought close to $200 billion.
Asked if Republicans had offered to accept a $140 billion tax cut, Lott told reporters, "We could live with that."
"They are still wanting less than we can agree to. We are saying we realise we are probably not going to get it in the $197 billion range," Lott added.
An administration official who asked not to be identified noted that $140 billion was well above what Clinton proposed and said there had been no agreements on actual numbers.
"We have not agreed to any numbers; they have not agreed to any numbers; but there is a sense of movement," said the official, adding, "We're not too close."
The timing of a deal, if one can be reached, is also up in the air.
The president's chief negotiator, Office of Management and Budget Director Frank Raines, told a Senate hearing Wednesday that he hoped for a budget in a few weeks.
Asked about the remark, McCurry said: "He is participating directly in the talks so I think that's pretty authoritative."
